claims.text: The initial catalyst is a near-equiatomic multi-principal-element alloy consisting primarily of Cu, Ni, Pd, and Pt.
The initial Cu–Ni–Pd–Pt catalyst has minimal platinum-group-metal content.
Cu, Ni, Pd, and Pt are uniformly distributed in the initial catalyst.
Sn precursor treatment followed by thermal diffusion at 250–300 °C for 1–2 hours will form a tin-enriched surface layer.
Controlled Sn loading can produce uniform surface modification without blocking active sites.
Sn shifts the d-band center or otherwise modifies the electronic state of nearby active-metal sites.
The Sn-induced electronic modification enhances adsorption of oxygen species needed for oxidation.
The Sn-enriched surface weakens adsorption of H2O.
The Sn-enriched surface weakens adsorption of NO.
Sn doping enhances CO and hydrocarbon oxidation below 150 °C relative to the unmodified catalyst.
Sn doping reduces activity loss caused by H2O and NO under simulated automotive exhaust.
Sn-induced electronic modification promotes surface self-healing during aging.
Sn doping retards sintering and produces a slower degradation rate during extended operation and accelerated aging.
Excessive Sn loading may aggregate or block active sites and reduce performance.
The intervention should remain effective during transient low-temperature automotive operation and aging stresses representative of a vehicle lifetime.

contradictions.description: Describing Cu, Ni, Pd, and Pt as the primary near-equiatomic constituents implies that the two platinum-group metals, Pd and Pt, constitute roughly half of the alloy, which conflicts with the simultaneous description of the material as having minimal platinum-group-metal content.
